text_blocks.snippet: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which strains the right side of the heart.
snippet_highlighted_words: high blood pressure in the lung arteries

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea): Often starts during physical exertion, such as walking or climbing stairs, and worsens over time.
Fatigue and weakness: Persistent tiredness caused by the heart struggling to pump enough oxygen-rich blood through the body.
Chest pain or pressure: Can occur during exertion or rest due to the overworked heart muscle.
Palpitations or fast pulse: A rapid, pounding, or irregular heartbeat as the heart tries to keep up with demand.
Dizziness or lightheadedness: Especially during physical activity.
Swelling (edema): Fluid buildup causing swollen ankles, legs, or a bloated abdomen as blood backs up toward the liver and heart.
Fainting (syncope): Occurs when the heart cannot supply enough blood flow to the brain, frequently triggered by exertion.
Bluish lips or skin (cyanosis): A sign of low oxygen levels in the blood.

text_blocks.snippet: Because early symptoms resemble asthma or other common lung and heart conditions, PAH can be difficult to catch right away. To learn more about diagnostic tests like echocardiograms or find patient resources, visit the American Lung Association Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Guide or consult the Mayo Clinic Pulmonary Hypertension Overview.
